source: ORIGINAL IELTS PAPERS – VOL 2, Writing Task 2 bonus bank

writing.title: Human activities and species loss
writing.prompt:
Write about the following topic:

Human activities have negative effects on plant and animal species. Some people think it is too late to do anything about this problem. Others believe that effective measures can be taken to improve this situation.

Discuss both views and give your opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample:
Human activities, such as deforestation and urbanisation, have narrowed the space available to other species on Earth and even threatened their existence. Some believe the damage is irreversible and that nothing can be done, whereas others insist that effective measures can still alleviate the situation. This essay examines both perspectives; personally, I side with the latter view.

Those who say nothing can be done to address the loss of animal and plant species give the following reasons. Firstly, they point to species that have already been lost and cannot be brought back: the southern Andean toad became extinct in 1968, and a Sri Lankan legume tree died out completely in the 1980s. They also argue that even if such species were revived, there would be no room for them to survive in today's world – the dinosaurs are a good example, since there is no longer any habitat in which they could proliferate. Finally, they claim that it is futile to protect weak species unless those species can sustain themselves.

On the other hand, the main argument for taking action is that simple steps would allow species on the verge of extinction to breed and recover. If the over-exploitation of natural resources were reduced, hunting and smuggling of wild animals banned, overgrazing and over-cultivation stopped, and afforestation encouraged, many species would not disappear.

I believe that we should not give up hope. There are many successful initiatives by governments and NGOs which prove that effort pays off. The Royal Bengal tiger, India's national animal, was once close to extinction, but a government programme supported by NGOs and public donations to the 'Save the Tiger' project has succeeded in raising its numbers. Other measures, such as using prefabricated materials for doors and windows, have reduced the felling of trees for timber.

To sum up, although human activity has done great harm to plant and animal species, it is not too late to make a start. We may not be able to reverse the damage already done, but we can prevent a great deal of further damage that is otherwise imminent.

writing.title: Traditional foods replaced by fast food
writing.prompt:
Write about the following topic:

In many countries traditional foods are being replaced by international fast food. This is having a negative effect on both families and societies.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample:
In this era of technology and globalisation, every sphere of life has changed dramatically, and food is no exception. I agree that international fast food chains have eaten into traditional cuisines, and that this has had a detrimental effect on families and societies. Several arguments support my opinion.

International fast food has many damaging effects on families. Firstly, at today's torrid pace of life, people work extremely long hours and have no time to prepare and enjoy traditional home-cooked food, so they switch to the easy option of restaurants; McDonald's has become a household name. Secondly, there is the growing influence of Western culture over local ones, and people are forgetting their roots. In the past, all family members sat together to eat, and over the dining table they shared the events of their day. Fast food is mostly eaten alone, partly because it does not appeal to the palate of older family members, and as a result family bonds are weakening and the art of home cooking is in decline.

Admittedly, the trend also harms individuals. Fast food is rich in fats and salt, which leads to obesity, and obesity is the root cause of many other illnesses: an obese person is far more likely to suffer from hypertension and diabetes.

There are tangible consequences for society too. Broadly speaking, as people turn to fast food and restaurants, local culture dies out, because traditional food is inextricably linked with culture. The identity of a society may gradually be replaced by a homogenised Western one. Furthermore, if people are not healthy, national productivity suffers. Last but not least, fast food promotes a use-and-throw culture, which adds to the problem of waste, pollution and, eventually, disease.

To summarise, international fast food has carved out its niche while traditional food has taken a back seat. This certainly has adverse effects on individuals, families and societies.

writing.title: Physical strength vs mental attitude in sport
writing.prompt:
Write about the following topic:

Some people believe that the fittest and strongest individuals and teams always succeed in sports. Others think that success in sports depends on mental attitude.

Discuss both views and give your opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample:
People are divided on the reasons for success in sport. Some believe that only the physically fit can succeed, while others argue that a positive mental attitude is what matters most. This essay discusses both views; I believe that both physical fitness and mental attitude are necessary for sporting success.

The main reason some people regard fitness and strength as decisive is that a player who is not physically fit cannot excel in sports such as rugby, football, wrestling or volleyball. This is why coaches and trainers make players work out for hours every day, so that they can build the strength and stamina their sport demands.

On the other hand, those who say that players succeed through a positive attitude and a good game plan cite players who have triumphed thanks to these virtues. Sachin Tendulkar, for example, is very short, yet he could do wonders with his bat. Anil Kumble, one of the best bowlers in cricket, could read the mind of the batsman facing him, and in one match he managed to take all ten wickets. In hockey, too, winning depends on teamwork, attitude and cooperation.

Furthermore, there are many examples of athletes who have reached the pinnacle of their careers despite severe physical limitations. The swimmer Amy Van Dyken suffered from asthma but went on to win Olympic gold medals; Jeff Blatnick recovered from cancer to win Olympic gold in Greco-Roman wrestling in 1984; and the Indian cricketer Yuvraj Singh fought lung cancer and returned to his team largely thanks to his positive mental attitude.

To sum up, physical fitness and strength undoubtedly play a role, but mental attitude is equally important. A successful sportsperson needs a combination of physical and mental power.

writing.title: Team activities vs solo activities
writing.prompt:
Write about the following topic:

Team activities can teach more skills for life than those activities which are played alone.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample:
Teamwork and individual work require different skills and teach different things. The statement claims that group activities are better teachers of life skills than solo activities. While I believe individual activities are important, team activities certainly have greater relevance.

Many significant skills are learnt only by working in a group, such as communication, cooperation and conflict management. In solo activities people do not need to communicate, so they do not develop these abilities; yet when they step into daily life, they realise that communication is the skill they need most. They must also cooperate with family members, colleagues, friends and neighbours, and team activities teach exactly this. Conflict management is another skill learnt in teams: people have differences of opinion, and they learn to handle difficult situations diplomatically.

Furthermore, team activities broaden people's horizons, as they interact with people from diverse backgrounds. Individuals learn how to make their voice heard and how to accept the suggestions of others. Finally, they learn sportsmanship – accepting victory with modesty and defeat with grace – which is an important life skill.

On the other hand, people do acquire valuable skills through solo activities, such as a sense of competition and perseverance. All life skills matter. However, we cannot forget that humans are social animals and cannot live alone. Especially today, with the division of labour, people are more dependent on one another than ever before. Success in life depends on how we deal with others and how we adapt to working in different situations, and this is learnt only by working with other people.

To conclude, both team and individual activities teach important life skills, but the skills learnt by working with others are of far greater importance.

writing.title: Rising demand for food
writing.prompt:
Write about the following topic:

Demand for food is increasing worldwide. What are the causes of this?

What measures can the international community take to make sure the supply of food is enough?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample:
Meeting the food needs of billions of people is going to be a major challenge in the years to come. This essay discusses the reasons for the growing demand for food and suggests some steps that can be taken at a global level to meet it.

There are several reasons for the rising demand. The most prominent is the unprecedented growth in the global population. Over the last century the population has quadrupled: it was under two billion in 1915, whereas today it exceeds seven billion and is expected to rise further. The second major cause is rising incomes in developing countries, which bring dietary changes such as the consumption of more protein and meat.

To address this potential food shortage, businesses and governments will have to work together. Firstly, farmers must be given assistance to produce more on the land they already farm, through more intensive and efficient methods. Demand for dairy products can also be met with modern technology: in India, millions of animals are needed to satisfy consumer demand for milk, whereas in America far fewer animals produce more milk thanks to the latest breeding and farming techniques.

Another step that could go a long way is reducing food waste. Information campaigns can make people aware of the scale of the waste and of how their habits of preparing and consuming food could change. New technologies can also minimise waste in storage and transport. It has been estimated that if food waste were halved over the next forty years, agricultural production would need to increase by only 45% instead of 70% – a far easier goal to achieve.

To sum up, there are many reasons for the increase in demand for food around the world, but there are equally many steps that can be taken to ensure the world's population is fed.
